sense: to do with trade; run for profit

evidence: Liv. 39.25: maritimum emporium … quaestuōsum et frūgiferum
terms.comment: What brings in money, from quaestus, gain (Lewis & Short): a commercial venture is rēs quaestuōsa. Of a person it means greedy for gain, and Plautus uses quaestuōsa of a prostitute (Mil. 3.1.190, old numbering; Lewis & Short), so say it of the business, not of the people in it. Where English “commercial” only means “of trade”, Latin uses the genitive: mercātūrae, negōtiōrum (see business).

terms.gloss: a commercial town, a trading port, a market
evidence: M-O s.v. city (as commercial center), after Egger
terms.comment: From Greek; a place of trade, usually on the sea or a river (Lewis & Short).

terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut.; in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra
evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 2.3.2 (old numbering): nāvis mercātōria, a merchant ship (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short has it only from Plautus.

phrases.latin: … ūnum maritimum emporium fuisse quondam Thessalīs quaestuōsum et frūgiferum
phrases.english: … that it had once been the Thessalians’ one seaport, a profitable and productive place of trade

sources: Lewis & Short: quaestuosus · Lewis & Short: emporium · Lewis & Short: mercatorius
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. city (as commercial center).
